sources.title: Letters to Olga (Havel's own prison correspondence, 1979-1982)
RFE/RL: "Havel Stepping Down As Czech President" -- documents the July 1992 resignation and his own quoted statement
Britannica's accounts of the Velvet Revolution and Havel's presidency

risk_tolerance.rationale: Three separate imprisonments as a direct, foreseeable consequence of his sustained dissident writing and organizing activity (a 40-month sentence for his role in Charter 77, a further four-and-a-half-year sentence in 1979 for "subversion of the republic," and a third separate imprisonment), including a nearly four-year continuous term from May 1979 to April 1983 -- an extreme, repeated, well-documented pattern of accepting severe personal cost for principle.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: Co-authored and led Charter 77 directly confronting the ruling government's human-rights record, sustained this confrontation across three imprisonments over more than a decade, and later publicly opposed the Czechoslovak federal split against the prevailing political momentum driven by both republics' prime ministers.

leadership_drive.rationale: Served as chief spokesman of Civic Forum during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, leading pro-democracy demonstrations that forced the communist government into negotiation, and was elected interim president within weeks (December 29, 1989), then re-elected in July 1990 -- an extraordinarily rapid, documented transition from imprisoned dissident to head of state within a single year.

persistence.rationale: Sustained substantive intellectual and reflective work, later published as Letters to Olga, through nearly four continuous years of imprisonment under severe communication restriction (one censored letter per week, forbidden from writing about his prison experience or political subjects), rather than disengaging intellectually.

independent_thinking.rationale: Two independent documented instances: became a leading absurdist playwright developing a distinctive theatrical voice before any political career, with his own plays later specifically banned from the stage; and took a position opposing the Czechoslovak federal split in 1992 when the prevailing political direction, driven by Klaus and Meciar, favored dissolution.

decisiveness.rationale: Resigned the presidency on July 20, 1992 at a precisely, symbolically chosen moment -- minutes before the Slovak Parliament declared sovereignty -- explaining in his own words that he could no longer honor his oath to defend the common state, rather than remaining in office through the transition.

creative_originality.rationale: Recognized, by his own stated artistic kinship with Beckett, Ionesco, Pinter, and Stoppard, and by the historical record of his own plays being specifically singled out and banned by the state, as a genuine, distinctive voice within European absurdist theater, inferred as real creative originality from this documented recognition.

provenance.notes: Roster-1000 session 15 (tightly controlled 4-person calibration experiment, docs/roster-1000-checkpoint.md Sec.81): selected specifically for domain breadth (political/social leadership) AND for an unusually well-documented public life. 5 substantive sources consulted (Wikipedia for orientation only, plus 4 independent sources: the Journal of Democracy's retrospective, Havel's own published prison letters, RFE/RL's account of his 1992 resignation including his own quoted statement, and Britannica's account of the Velvet Revolution). Evidence ledger: 14 distinct, source-attributed episodes, spanning at least 4 life periods (the pre-political playwriting career, the Charter 77/imprisonment period, the 1989 revolution and presidency, the 1992 resignation) and at least 5 behavioral contexts (solitary creative work, sustained public conflict, interpersonal/reflective expression under duress, formal leadership, a single decisive principled act). Ledger built and locked BEFORE any trait score was assigned; trait scores locked BEFORE eligibility_v2 was consulted.
